title.heading: Why the Romans built Hadrian’s Wall
title.lead: What can a wall keep out?

picture.shows: Hadrian’s Wall at Walltown Crags in Northumberland today, in colour
picture.subject: named

slides.heading: Hadrian’s northern frontier
slides.lead: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian ordered work on his wall.
points: The wall crossed what is now northern England.
It stretched from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth.

figure.shows: A geographically accurate outline map of Britain showing Hadrian’s Wall across northern England, with Scotland north of it and the two endpoints labelled. This is a location map, not a reconstruction.

slides.heading: Why build a wall?
slides.lead: The wall marked the northern frontier of Roman Britain.
points: It made raids by groups from northern Britain harder by blocking easy crossings.
Roman soldiers could direct travellers towards guarded gates and check who crossed.

cards.label: Key word
cards.meaning: A border between lands controlled by different groups.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of Hadrian’s Wall with a guarded gateway, travellers approaching along a track and open countryside north of the wall
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Places for soldiers to guard
slides.lead: Roman soldiers guarded the wall from different buildings.
points: Forts housed hundreds of soldiers who could respond to danger.
Milecastles were small forts about one Roman mile apart.
Gates let soldiers stop travellers and check their goods.

cards.label: Wall building
cards.meaning: A small fort with a guarded gateway.

figure.shows: A reconstruction showing a large Roman fort beside Hadrian’s Wall and, farther along, a small milecastle with soldiers at its gateway. Labels belong outside the picture.
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: How did gates help Roman soldiers control the frontier?

options.text: They channelled travellers through places where soldiers could check them.
They kept every traveller outside because nobody could cross the wall.
options.why: The pupil treats the wall as a complete ban on movement rather than a way to control crossings.

options.text: They let travellers cross wherever they wanted while soldiers stayed inside.
options.why: The pupil recognises that crossing was possible but misses the purpose of guarded crossing points.

slides.heading: Watching the gaps
slides.lead: Soldiers also watched the stretches of wall between milecastles.
points: Small towers called turrets stood between the milecastles.
Soldiers patrolled along the frontier to watch for danger.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of a Roman turret beside Hadrian’s Wall, with a soldier watching from its upper level and other soldiers patrolling beside the wall
figure.subject: generic

items.question: A trader brings wool towards Roman Britain from the north. How could soldiers use a gate to control entry?
items.answer: Soldiers could stop the trader at the gate and check the wool before allowing entry.

items.question: A group approaches the wall far from a gate. How could turrets and a nearby fort help soldiers respond?
items.answer: Soldiers in turrets could spot the group, and soldiers from the fort could go to meet it.

items.question: Which emperor ordered work on the wall?
What small forts stood along the wall’s route?
What were the small watching towers called?
When and where did Hadrian order his wall to be built?
items.answer: In AD 122, across what is now northern England, from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth.

items.question: Why was a guarded gate more useful than an unguarded gap?
items.answer: Soldiers could check travellers at a guarded gate, but an unguarded gap would let groups cross freely.

items.question: How did forts and milecastles each help Roman soldiers guard Hadrian’s Wall?
items.answer: Forts housed many soldiers who could respond to danger, while milecastles guarded gateways along the wall.
